Integer Programming 2: Larger Models and Worked Problems¶

The first chapter solved small integer programs with the dense branch-and-bound. Real integer models are bigger, have a mix of whole and continuous variables, and benefit from a stronger search. This chapter introduces the sparse branch-and-cut solver and uses it on two complete problems: choosing where to open warehouses, and building a weekly staff schedule. After it you can pick between the two integer solvers, read the extra result fields, and verify an integer answer without trusting the solver that found it.

Every program is complete and its output is the output of that program.

The mental model¶

The sparse solver, lp::solve_mip(model, options), is a branch-and-cut method. It is branch and bound with three additions that make the search much shorter.

  • Presolve shrinks the model first, as for a linear program (chapter 4).

  • Cutting planes are extra constraints, valid for every integer solution but violated by the relaxation’s fractional answer, added at the root to tighten the bound before any branching.

  • Heuristics (diving, and small sub-integer-programs around the relaxation) look for good integer solutions early, so that more of the tree can be pruned.

Its MipResult has the same essentials as the dense one, status, objective, x, best_bound and nodes, and adds the relative gap and lp_iterations. A search that ends with nodes = 0 was finished at the root: presolve, the cuts and the heuristics together closed the gap before any branching.

MipOptions

Meaning

Default

node_limit

stop after this many nodes

very large

rel_gap, abs_gap

stop when the bound and the incumbent agree to this

1e-6, 1e-9

int_tol

how close to whole counts as whole

1e-6

presolve

true

cut_rounds

rounds of cutting planes at the root (0 turns them off)

25

heuristics

diving and sub-integer-program heuristics

true

A dense milp::Problem is solved with the sparse engine by lp::solve_sparse(problem). The two engines must agree on the optimal value, and when they do on a model you built, that is good evidence the model is as you meant.

Programs¶

  • Larger integer models

A routine for an integer program¶

  1. Write the model with the relaxation in mind: tight bounds on every integer variable, and capacities linked to decisions as tightly as the problem allows (the capacity times y in Program 1 is the tightest valid link; a very large constant in its place would give a weak relaxation and a long search).

  2. Solve the relaxation first. If it is whole, you are done; if not, its value is a bound on the answer.

  3. Solve the integer program. Read the status, then objective and best_bound. If the search ended on a node limit, the gap between them is your measure of quality.

  4. Check the plan against the constraints directly, row by row, from the data.

  5. Verify optimality by something independent: brute force on a small instance, enumeration of the integer part, a counting bound, or the other engine.

What to remember¶

  • Branch-and-cut adds presolve, cutting planes and heuristics to branch and bound. It reports the same essentials plus the relative gap.

  • nodes = 0 means the search was closed at the root.

  • Link a capacity to its decision variable as tightly as you can; a loose link weakens the relaxation.

  • Verify an integer answer independently: enumerate the integer part and solve the rest as a linear program, or count.

  • Dense and sparse engines must agree on the optimum of a well-formed model.
